item.title: Large language and atomic model: bridging atomistic representation and language reasoning for accelerating materials discovery
item.description:
npj Artificial Intelligence · Xiaoyue He, Bowen Hou, Hongyu Wu, Jianbo Hu, Lu Zhang, Lipeng Chen
The combination of artificial intelligence and materials science promises accelerated discovery, yet existing approaches remain limited by a fundamental divide between physically grounded prediction and flexible reasoning. Large atomic models provide accurate structure-property relationships but are computationally expensive and lack general reasoning capability, whereas large language models excel at abstraction and inference but struggle with structured physical representations and reliable quantitative prediction. Efforts to bridge these paradigms have been impeded by competing training objectives: atomic models demand precise numerical optimization, while reasoning requires coherent sequential inference; when forced into a single objective, these requirements interfere, degrading both predictive fidelity and logical consistency. Here we introduce a Large Language and Atomic Model (LLAM), a multimodal framework with native structural reasoning capability that directly integrates atomistic representations with language-based inference. By aligning atomistic representations with the language embedding space through a lightweight cross-modal bridge, LLAM conditions both quantitative prediction and subsequent reasoning directly on crystal structures. Across diverse benchmarks spanning continuous property prediction and crystallographic classification, LLAM demonstrates strong performance while exhibiting improved reasoning capability. Case studies in optoelectronic-property interpretation, solid-state electrolyte optimization, and photovoltaic-material screening further demonstrate that LLAM can connect structure-grounded predictions with physically meaningful interpretations and application-oriented decisions.

item.title: Autapse-inspired neuromorphic hardware with synapse–neuron integration for bidirectional feedback control
item.description:
Nature Communications · Chan Kim, Seonkwon Kim, Jeong Hwan Song, Jongyoung Lee, Leejae Kim, Seongil Im
Abstract Establishing autonomous and energy-efficient feedback control at the hardware level remains challenging because conventional systems rely on centralized processing and continuous external computation, increasing energy consumption and system complexity. Here we show a neuromorphic autapse-inspired system that enables localized and bidirectional feedback control, using thermoregulation as a representative application. An autapse is a self-synaptic connection in which a neuron feeds its output back to its own synaptic input, enabling intrinsic feedback modulation. The system integrates a solid electrolyte-based synaptic transistor capable of multiplexing multiple inputs and a bidirectional leaky integrate-and-fire artificial neuron. By feeding the neuronal output back to an additional synaptic gate, excitatory and inhibitory feedback loops are realized within a compact architecture. Using an artificial thermoregulation platform, temperature-dependent inputs bidirectionally modulate neuronal firing frequency, demonstrating biologically inspired feedback control with a compact set of neuromorphic devices for autonomous and energy-efficient systems.

item.title: Comment on “Self-organizing neuromorphic nanowire networks as stochastic dynamical systems"
item.description:
Nature Communications · Renat Timergalievich Sibatov, П.О. Ксенофонтова
Self-assembled networks of nano-objects have attracted growing interest as physical substrates for brain-inspired computation. The work of Milano et al. 1 is a valuable study of the dynamics of memristive networks of nanowires. The experimental data presented by the authors are comprehensive and of high quality, providing extensive material for validating stochastic conductance models in such systems. The compact Markovian model proposed in ref. 1 , formulated as a stochastic differential equation of the Itô type that combines deterministic return to equilibrium with random components (Gaussian noise and jumps), allows for the description of certain aspects of the dynamics and an assessment of the impact of stochasticity on computational capabilities within the reservoir computing paradigm. However, closer examination of the data from ref. 1 reveals that each key aspect of the conductance dynamics (deterministic relaxation, jump process, and Gaussian fluctuations) exhibits non-Markovian properties, which calls into question the original stochastic model and suggests a need for its fundamental revision.

item.title: MultiSHAP: a Shapley-based framework for explaining cross-modal interactions in multimodal AI models
item.description:
npj Artificial Intelligence · Zhanliang Wang, Kai Wang
Abstract Multimodal AI models have achieved impressive performance in tasks that require integrating information from multiple modalities, such as vision and language. While existing model explanation methods, such as attention maps and Grad-CAM, offer insights into cross-modal relationships, they do not explicitly quantify fine-grained interactions between individual visual and textual elements and require access to model internals. Here we introduce MultiSHAP, an architecture-agnostic interpretability framework that leverages the Shapley Interaction Index to attribute multimodal outputs to pairwise interactions between fine-grained visual and textual elements, such as image patches and text tokens. MultiSHAP does not require access to model parameters, gradients, attention weights, or intermediate representations, but requires a query interface that permits separate perturbation of visual and textual inputs and returns a task-relevant scalar score, either directly or through a ranked output from which such a score can be deterministically constructed. Our approach provides: (1) instance-level explanations that characterize how specific visual and textual elements jointly affect a selected model output, and (2) dataset-level descriptive summaries of interaction patterns under a specified model, value function, feature partition, and masking operator. Experiments on multimodal benchmarks provide evidence that MultiSHAP captures behaviorally relevant input-level interactions, while pair-level evaluations provide partial evidence that the estimated patch–token correspondences contain information beyond unimodal saliency, and case studies illustrate its use for examining individual multimodal decisions. Although evaluated here on vision–language models, the underlying interaction formulation may in principle be extended to other modality combinations.

item.title: Redundancy maximization as a principle of associative memory learning in Hopfield networks
item.description:
Nature Communications · Mark Blümel, Andreas C. Schneider, Valentin Neuhaus, David A. Ehrlich, Marcel Graetz, Michael Wibral
Associative memory, traditionally modeled by Hopfield networks, enables the retrieval of previously stored patterns from partial or noisy cues. Yet, the local computational principles which are required to enable this function remain incompletely understood. To formally characterize the local information processing in such systems, we employ a recent extension of information theory-Partial Information Decomposition. It decomposes the contribution of different inputs to an output into unique information from each input, redundant information across inputs, and synergistic information that emerges from combining different inputs. Applying this framework to individual neurons in classical Hopfield networks we find that below the memory capacity, the information in a neuron's activity is characterized by high redundancy between the external pattern input and the internal recurrent input, while synergy and unique information are close to zero until the memory capacity is surpassed and performance drops steeply. Inspired by this observation, we use redundancy maximization at each neuron as an information-theoretic learning goal. This increases the network's memory capacity to 1.59, a more than tenfold improvement over the 0.14 capacity of classical Hopfield networks, and also outperforming recent state-of-the-art implementations of Hopfield networks. Overall, this work establishes redundancy maximization as a design principle for associative memories and opens pathways for new associative memory models based on information-theoretic goals.

item.title: Autoplastic neural network: self-evolving networks with dynamic connectivity and modality adaptation
item.description:
npj Artificial Intelligence · Matthew Korban, Peter A. Youngs, Scott T. Acton
Abstract Deep networks are usually built first and trained later, forcing fixed capacity and wasted compute. We introduce the Autoplastic Neural Network, a training-time framework that learns structure and weights together. Layer inclusion, neuron-level connectivity, and per-layer operation mixing are jointly optimized within a fixed maximal supernetwork, whose pre-allocated components are reinforced or pruned as learning progresses; the resulting model supports per-input routing and can also be exported as a compact static architecture. A stability-gated rule coordinates architectural changes with gradient descent and yields convergence guarantees. Across vision, video, language, bioinformatics, and healthcare tasks, the approach surpasses strong static and dynamic baselines while using less computation. Unlike neural architecture search, no outer search loop is required; evolution happens inside a single learning process with cost comparable to training a single model. By unifying optimization and design, Autoplastic networks allocate capacity where needed, remove redundancy when possible, and deliver practical, resource-aware deep learning.

item.title: High-performance annealing-free wurtzite ferroelectric field-effect transistors with ultrathin oxide semiconductors for neuromorphic computing
item.description:
Nature Communications · Kai Wang, Tingting Gao, 胡凯生, Suyuan Cai, Huibo Liu, Haotian Liang
Wurtzite-structured aluminum scandium nitride (AlScN) ferroelectric materials are potential candidates for non-volatile memory (NVM) applications because of their high remanent polarization (Pr > 100 μC·cm−2) and compatibility with back-end-of-line (BEOL) processes. However, achieving high-performance wurtzite ferroelectric field-effect transistors (FeFETs) remains a significant challenge because of their high interface trap density (Dit) and large threshold voltage (VTH) variation. Here we show the distinct polarization switching mechanisms of AlScN FeFETs based on an ultrathin indium gallium oxide (IGO) channel with three different structures. FeFETs with a metal–ferroelectric–metal–insulator–semiconductor (MFMIS) structure show high interface quality with low Dit and a stable VTH, achieving a large memory window (MW) of up to 20.6 V and a high endurance of 106. The stable 6-bit operation of our devices with 64 distinct states shows the feasibility of multilevel storage applications. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of the FeFET in neuromorphic networks, with a high recognition accuracy of 93.02%. AlScN field-effect transistors for non-volatile memory are limited by high interface trap density and threshold voltage instability. Wang et al. demonstrate annealing-free AlScN ferroelectric transistors with low interface trap density and stable threshold voltage, enabling a large memory window and robust 6-bit operation.

item.title: No-go theorems for sublinear-depth group designs
item.description:
Nature Communications · Maxwell West, Diego García-Martín, N. L. Diaz, M. Cerezo, Martin Larocca
Constructing ensembles of circuits which efficiently approximate the Haar measure over various groups is a fundamental problem in quantum information theory, with breakthrough recent results showing that for the unitary group this can be achieved with depths scaling logarithmically in the system size. Here we prove that, for groups G possessing an invariant state $${G}^{\otimes k}\left\vert \Psi \right\rangle=\left\vert \Psi \right\rangle$$ satisfying certain conditions on its entanglement structure, no subset of G consisting of sublinear-depth one-dimensional circuits with constant-locality gates can form an approximate k-design over G. More generally, on a D-dimensional lattice of side-length n, our results imply that such group designs require depths scaling at least as n1/D. Among other examples, we show that there is a constant separation between the maximum depth and gate counts for which no circuit can approximate even the second moment of random matchgate circuits, and those required to implement the matchgate Haar distribution exactly. Finally, we relax the assumption of working with local gates, and prove the impossibility of obtaining approximate designs over G using any circuit comprised of a sublinear number of gates generated by Pauli strings. Significant effort has been spent to find low-depth constructions of random unitaries that appear Haar-random to a restricted observer, and earlier works showed logarithmic-depth approximate designs over the full unitary group using local random circuits. In this paper, the authors provide a general criterion ruling out shallow designs on a wide variety of groups.

item.title: HuBMAP Data Portal: a resource for multimodal spatial and single-cell data of healthy human tissues
item.description:
Nature Communications · Morgan L. Turner, Thomas Chris Smits, Tiffany Sun Liaw, Brendan John Honick, Bill Shirey, Lisa Choy
The NIH Human BioMolecular Atlas Program (HuBMAP) Data Portal ( https://portal.hubmapconsortium.org/ ) serves as a comprehensive repository for multimodal, multi-scale spatial and single-cell data from healthy human tissues. As of August 2026, the portal hosts 9,316 public datasets from 26 data types spanning 29 organ classes across 501 donors. Portal infrastructure and user interfaces support data search and discovery, visualization, and analysis directly in web browsers. These capabilities include metadata- and data-driven search, collaborative Workspaces with access to high-performance compute, and interactive Vitessce visualizations across non-spatial, 2D, and 3D spatial datasets. Data-type-specific uniform processing pipelines and rigorous quality control processes ensure comparability of results across laboratories, organs, and donors, while externally processed community-contributed datasets provide complementary perspectives. Here we describe portal functionality, infrastructure, and design, and highlight its role as a platform for large-scale spatial single-cell research across diverse data types, organs, and scales.

item.title: Learning What the Operator Misses: Residual Operator-Diffusion for Spatiotemporal PDE Solution Predictions

item.title: CADS: a comprehensive anatomical dataset and segmentation for whole-body anatomy in computed tomography
item.description:
Nature Communications · Murong Xu, Fernando Navarro, Maksym Fritsak, İbrahim Ethem Hamamcı, Suprosanna Shit, Bastian Wittmann
Abstract Volumetric computed tomography (CT) segmentation supports quantitative image analysis, but most AI-based methods remain organ-specific, with fragmented models, inconsistent label definitions, and heterogeneous training and evaluation protocols. Here we present CADS, a unified data–model framework for scalable and generalizable whole-body CT segmentation. We construct a SNOMED-CT-referenced anatomical label space harmonizing heterogeneous cohorts from over 100 imaging centers, yielding complete annotations of 167 structures across 22,022 CT volumes and markedly expanding anatomical coverage and scale beyond existing resources. To complete labels on sparsely annotated CTs, we combine self-training with shape-informed quality control based on neural implicit functions, curating high-quality pseudo-labels. Trained on this resource, CADS shows robust whole-body segmentation across distribution shifts and improved performance relative to state-of-the-art approaches across 18 public datasets. We further validate it in an independent, expert-reviewed real-world oncology cohort of 2864 CTs. The curated dataset, pretrained models, and user-friendly software together provide an accessible, reproducible foundation for large-scale anatomical segmentation and computational anatomy research.

item.title: Inflammatory memory primes the intestine for enhanced regenerative potential
item.description:
Nature Communications · Borja Arozamena, Ilias Moraitis, Loris Mularoni, Olga Wienskowska, Jasin Taelman, Milica Stefanović
How do inflammation and activation of the regenerative genetic program affect intestinal epithelial cell behavior and shape responses to future injuries? Following injury, which typically induces intestinal stem cell (ISC) death, regeneration occurs via the proliferation of surviving ISCs and via cellular plasticity through dedifferentiation of progenitors and committed cells. While inflammation and cellular plasticity are hallmarks of regeneration, its long-term effects on epithelial cell behavior are not well understood. Using single cell multiomics, we demonstrate that inflammatory exposure and cellular plasticity imprint a lasting transcriptional and epigenetic memory on ISCs and their progeny, priming them for enhanced repair after subsequent injuries. Mechanistically, we identify IFN-γ as a critical driver of this primed regenerative state. These findings uncover how prior inflammation reprograms regenerative capacity, with implications for tissue resilience and disease susceptibility. The intestine remembers past injury. Arozamena and colleagues reveal that transcriptional and epigenetic memory accelerates future repair, with IFN-gamma encoding inflammatory memory and dedifferentiation leaving a distinct regenerative imprint.

item.title: Emergence of diffusion models from associative memory through memorization and generalization
item.description:
Nature Communications · Bao Pham, Gabriel Raya, Matteo Negri, Mohammed Javeed Zaki, Luca Ambrogioni, Dmitry Krotov
Abstract Dense Associative Memories (DenseAMs) are generalizations of Hopfield networks that store training data at local minima of the energy landscape. When the amount of training data exceeds the critical memory storage capacity, new local minima (different from the training data) emerge. These emergent local minima, known as spurious states, can hinder memory retrieval. We examine diffusion models (DMs) through the DenseAM lens, viewing their generative process as an attempt of a memory retrieval. In the small data regime, DMs create distinct attractors for each training sample, akin to DenseAMs below the critical capacity. As the training set size increases, DMs transition to generalization. We identify a critical intermediate phase, predicted by DenseAM theory, characterized by the emergence of spurious states. In generative modeling, these previously overlooked states are no longer negative artifacts but rather are the first signs of generative capabilities. Their existence is demonstrated across a wide range of architectures and datasets.

item.title: Evaluating anonymized genome re-identification using polygenic predictions and its implications for data privacy
item.description:
Nature Communications · Théo Cavinato, Robin J. Hofmeister, Zoltán Kutalik
Abstract Re-identification by phenotypic prediction aims to determine whether a genome belongs to a specific individual by comparing the individual’s known traits with those predicted from the genome. Although this tracing attack is widely discussed in the genomic privacy literature, its practical risk remains uncertain. As genome-wide association studies (GWAS) continue to improve phenotypic prediction, concerns about the potential for this attack increase. Here, to quantify its real-world threat, we develop a probabilistic framework that estimates the likelihood of a match between an individual’s observed traits and polygenic scores (PGS) derived from a genome, while accounting for prediction accuracy and genetic and environmental correlations between traits. We benchmark this re-identification method and examine how the prior probability that a random genome and set of traits correspond to the same person affects performance. Finally, we assess whether sensitive genetic information, such as APOE- ε 4 status (linked with Alzheimer’s disease) can be inferred through this attack. Our method outperforms a state-of-the-art tool, reaching a precision above 99% for a recall of 40% when considering a prior of 50%. However, in real-world settings, we estimate that realistic priors do not exceed 4 × 10 −4 %, resulting in a precision lower than 0.13% at the same recall. Inference of sensitive genetic variants also proves ineffective: precision above 50% for identifying APOE- ε 4 carriers is achieved only at a recall below 20%. Thus, although re-identification by phenotypic prediction is technically feasible, its effectiveness in real-world conditions remains limited.

item.title: Enhancing bosonic qubit protection by squeezing
item.description:
Nature Communications · R. Rousseau, Diego Ruiz, E. Albertinale, P. d’Avezac, D. Banys, U. Blandin
Bosonic qubits implement error correction by harnessing the high-dimensional Hilbert space of a harmonic oscillator to redundantly encode logical quantum information. Squeezing of quantum states — a cornerstone of precision metrology — redistributes uncertainty between conjugate quadratures to enhance sensitivity in one variable at the expense of the other. In bosonic codes, decoherence can be seen as the environment performing an unwanted measurement on a noise-sensitive quadrature, collapsing superpositions and inducing errors. By redistributing uncertainty to that quadrature, squeezing can be leveraged to reduce the environment’s measurement strength, thereby prolonging coherence. Here, we exploit this insight to implement a squeezing deformation of the simplest bosonic code — the cat qubit — extending the bit-flip time with minimal impact on the phase-flip rate. We observe a dramatic reduction in bit-flip errors, achieving a 160-fold improvement over standard cat qubits and bringing multi-cat architectures closer to fault-tolerant quantum computation. In bosonic codes, decoherence can be seen as the environment performing an unwanted measurement on a noise-sensitive quadrature, collapsing superpositions and inducing errors. Here, the authors show how to use squeezing to further protect bosonic codes from noise, extending the bit-flip times of the cat qubit by two orders of magnitude without reducing phase-flip times.

item.title: Silk fibroin intrinsically activates Ccl27⁺ migratory-paracrine keratinocytes to orchestrate epidermal–dermal crosstalk for regenerative wound healing
item.description:
Nature Communications · Yue Zhu, Haoyang Liu, Yu Zhang, Jin Wang, Yanjin Mao, Ruoyu Zhao
Rapid and functional skin wound healing remains a major clinical challenge, while current biomaterial-based therapies largely serve as passive scaffolds or delivery vehicles. Whether biomaterials possess intrinsic bioactivities that instruct endogenous regenerative programs remains unclear. Here, independent of bulk structural/mechanical cues or exogenous biomolecules, we show that silk fibroin (SF), a clinically approved biomaterial, intrinsically programs keratinocytes into a Ccl27⁺ migratory-paracrine pro-regenerative state that coordinates epidermal-dermal crosstalk to drive regenerative wound healing. Integrated scRNA-seq, proteomics, and genetic perturbation reveal that SF engages keratinocyte ITGA2 to activate PI3K-Akt signaling and relieve P53-mediated Ccl27 repression. Elevated Ccl27 enhances keratinocyte migration and re-epithelialization, while its secretion from SF-activated keratinocytes promotes fibroblast proliferation and dermal remodeling, collectively enabling wound closure and appendage reconstruction. Keratinocyte-specific Ccl27 knockdown largely abrogates SF-mediated regeneration in vivo. These findings uncover the intrinsic bioactivity of SF and establish biomaterials as instructive cues rather than passive scaffolds for functional tissue repair. Biomaterials are widely used in wound care, but whether they can actively direct tissue repair remains not well understood. Here, authors show that silk fibroin intrinsically programs keratinocytes into a regenerative state that coordinates epidermal–dermal crosstalk and promotes wound healing.

item.title: Tensor-space joint optimisation of topology-role configuration in multi-agent systems
item.description:
Nature Communications · Changping Yu, Jiaming Zhang, Yang Liu, Yingmin Jia
Topology-role coupling is central to multi-agent formation control, yet its combinatorial complexity makes analytical treatment challenging. We propose a three-tensor framework that separately encodes graph structure, time-varying channel states, and role assignments. Their contraction yields a coupling metric equal to the mean of the non-trivial Laplacian eigenvalues, which serves as a tractable joint optimisation objective. Within this framework, the optimal leader emerges intrinsically from the tensor algebra, without recourse to heuristic rules or external designation. Optimisation is performed via spectral gradient flow restricted to a Tucker-compressed subspace, using incremental updates and warm starts from previous solutions. Under mild assumptions, Tucker compression guarantees polynomial complexity, and the gradient flow is proven to converge. Simulations demonstrate substantially better scaling than exhaustive combinatorial search as agent numbers grow. The framework unifies multi-agent control, graph theory, and tensor algebra, providing a principled foundation for scalable coordination in networked systems. Here, the authors develop a tensor-based framework for jointly optimizing communication topology and role assignment in multi-agent systems. They establish theoretical guarantees for the proposed optimization and demonstrate improved scalability and performance over combinatorial approaches.

item.title: Agentic inequality
item.description: Nature Machine Intelligence · Matthew Sharp, Omer Bilgin, Iason Gabriel, Lewis Hammond

item.title: Financial time-series generation: a systematic survey of taxonomy, evaluation, datasets, and open challenges
item.description:
npj Artificial Intelligence · Yingxiao Zhang, Jiaxin Duan, Yue Zou, Ke Feng, Jing Xiao
The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence has catalyzed a paradigm shift in quantitative finance, transitioning from traditional point forecasting toward comprehensive financial time-series generation (FTSG) across extrapolation, imputation, and full-scale data synthesis. This transition is motivated by the critical need to simulate rare market regimes, reconstruct incomplete historical records, and produce privacy-preserving synthetic environments for stress testing and trading execution. However, empirical financial properties—including heavy tails, volatility clustering, non-stationarity, and regime shifts—pose severe hurdles for generic generative frameworks. In this systematic survey, we review 131 studies from 2021 to early 2026 to bridge the gap between machine learning capabilities and econometric validity. We introduce a two-level taxonomy structuring the domain across task formulations and algorithmic families, and establish a multi-dimensional evaluation protocol encompassing distributional fidelity, stylized facts preservation, and downstream utility. Furthermore, we catalog curated financial databases and benchmark suites while addressing empirical dataset construction pitfalls. Finally, we identify pivotal open challenges in causal representation learning, econometrically bounded modeling, and online adaptation under distribution shifts. This review provides a standardized roadmap for developing robust, domain-aligned financial generative models.

item.title: The crystal ball problem: why prediction models are not guaranteed to improve health outcomes
item.description:
npj Artificial Intelligence · Leo Anthony Celi, Ryohei Yamamoto, Chrystinne Oliveira Fernandes, Eri Kobayashi, Aiden Liang, Heather Mattie
Clinical prediction rests on a seductive premise: accurate forecasts of deterioration will prompt earlier intervention and better outcomes. We argue that this assumption is not merely unproven but structurally flawed. The distinction between forecasting and decision evaluation is established yet routinely neglected. Using anticoagulation during extracorporeal membrane oxygenation as a case study, we show why predictive accuracy alone cannot establish clinical benefit, and how causal analysis of existing data can bridge validation and prospective impact trials.

item.title: Reusability report: multi-sample omics network inference operates in distinct robustness regimes defined by prior knowledge and data availability
item.description:
Nature Machine Intelligence · Xabier Martinez‐de‐Morentin, Sameer Ahmad Khan, Itziar Cenzano, Robert Lehmann, Alberto Maillo, Vincenzo Lagani
Abstract Knowledge-constrained network inference enables the reconstruction of regulatory programmes from high-dimensional biological data, yet the conditions under which shared and context-specific structures can be reliably identified remain poorly understood. Pablo Rodriguez-Mier et al. recently introduced CORNETO, a framework for multi-sample constrained inference. Here we reproduce, evaluate and extend CORNETO in terms of robustness, identifiability and bias–variance trade-offs. Using dynamic haematopoiesis and stable cortical datasets, we systematically assess four network reconstruction paradigms while preserving the original method-specific evaluation procedures and benchmark definitions. We show that multi-sample inference generally improves robustness and reproducibility, although gains in predictive performance depend on biological context and the completeness of the prior network. To enhance stability, we introduce bootstrap aggregation and selective re-expansion strategies that improve consensus robustness and recovery while preserving context-specific signals without modifying the underlying optimization scheme or sacrificing generality. Across datasets and methods, our results reveal distinct inference regimes governed by sample availability, prior knowledge and regularization. Together, these findings position network reconstruction as a regime-dependent learning problem and provide practical principles for robust multi-sample biological network inference.

item.title: Federated causal inference for effect estimation in healthcare: methods, challenges, and applications
item.description:
npj Artificial Intelligence · Haoyang Li, Zheqi Lyu, Meihan Wei, Simai Cheng, Wenhan Zheng, Fuying Ding
Federated causal inference enables treatment-effect estimation across healthcare systems without centralizing patient-level data. We review methods for binary, continuous, and time-to-event outcomes through three lenses: estimand, distributed-computation protocol, and privacy mechanism. We compare major strategies, clarify when federated analyses can approximate pooled results, and highlight unresolved challenges in confounding, heterogeneity, survival estimands, privacy–utility trade-offs, validation, and software. This framework supports rigorous evaluation of federated causal methods in healthcare.

item.title: LitGene: an interpretable transformer model integrating text and ontology for gene representation learning
item.description:
Nature Communications · Oladimeji Macaulay, Ala Jararweh, David Arredondo, Luis E. Tafoya, Shrey Poshiya, Yue Hu
Abstract Representation learning in genomics often relies on sequence, expression, and network data, thereby overlooking a wealth of insights in the scientific literature. Here, we present LitGene, an interpretable transformer-based model that refines gene representations by integrating unstructured textual information with Gene Ontology annotations through contrastive learning. In evaluations across eight benchmark tasks for protein properties, LitGene achieves competitive accuracy and exhibits zero-shot prediction of GO terms, KEGG pathways, and gene-disease associations. LitGene identified ANGPTL6 as a potential candidate gene for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), supported by its differential expression in independent IPF samples, illustrating LitGene’s utility for hypothesis generation. A SHAP-based interpretability tool highlights text features influencing predictions, while an automated literature-grounding framework provides corroborating support where available. Our results suggest that integrating textual and genetic information may help reduce biases associated with under-studied genes. The model is released as open-source code, along with a publicly accessible web interface at https://litgene.cs.unm.edu/ , which allows users to submit gene names, disease names, drug names, or custom text (e.g., publication abstracts) to obtain evidence-based predictions of related biomedical entities.

item.title: Large-scale iontronic skins with neural-hierarchical processing architecture
item.description:
Nature Machine Intelligence · Zhibin Li, Bingxu Da, Junli Shi, Taihong Wang, Wenlong Si, Wenlong Si
Abstract The human skin gathers and encodes signals from over 200,000 mechanoreceptors, enabling high-spatiotemporal-resolution tactile perception and instant injury prevention. Existing skin-like sensor arrays often have limited sensor count and density, and they use a serial readout architecture that suffers from readout latency, signal crosstalk and bandwidth consumption as element density increases. Here we report a high-density (1,110 units cm ‒2 ) and large-scale (>10,000 units) neural-hierarchical iontronic skin that mimics the hierarchical processing architecture of the human sensory system, which transmits interactive information in layers via signal encoding, convergence and cognitive modelling. Frequency-based position encoding of iontronic sensors enables parallel signal transmission with suppressed crosstalk and a rate of 100 frames per second, while backend convergent compression decreases bandwidth consumption by hundreds of times. We demonstrate that humanoid robots equipped with neural-hierarchical iontronic skins can perform challenging tasks, including fine tactile interactions that can resolve surface features of 300 µm, and the perception of nociceptive stimuli for self-protective responses. This technology provides a large-scale tactile system with high spatiotemporal resolution, paving the way for humanoid robots to approach human-level perception and manipulation.

item.title: Is there “Secret Sauce” in large language model development?
item.description:
npj Artificial Intelligence · Matthias Mertens, Natalia Fischl-Lanzoni, Neil Thompson
Abstract Do leading LLM developers possess a proprietary “secret sauce,” or is LLM performance driven by scaling up compute? Using training and benchmark data for 809 models released between 2022 and 2025, we estimate scaling-law regressions with release date and developer fixed effects. We find clear evidence of developer-specific efficiency advantages, but their importance depends on where models lie in the performance distribution. At the frontier, 80–90% of performance differences are explained by higher training compute, implying that scale—not proprietary technology—drives frontier advances. Away from the frontier, however, proprietary techniques and shared algorithmic progress substantially reduce the compute required to reach fixed capability thresholds. Some companies can systematically produce smaller models more efficiently. Strikingly, we also find substantial variation of model residual efficiency within companies; a firm can train two models with more than 40x compute efficiency difference. We also discuss the implications for AI leadership and capability diffusion.

item.title: Continuous-time noise mitigation in analogue quantum simulation
item.description:
Nature Communications · Gabriele Bressanini, Yue Ma, Michael Hanks, Hyukjoon Kwon, M. S. Kim
Analogue quantum simulators offer a promising route to explore quantum many-body dynamics beyond classical reach in the near term. However, their vulnerability to noise limits the accuracy of simulations. Here, we establish a continuous-time framework for mitigating noise in analogue quantum simulation. Our protocol fully preserves the continuous-time nature by avoiding any active control or measurement of the system during the dynamics, while achieving exact noise cancellation. This requires a small number of ancillary qubits, whose interaction with the system, combined with classical post-processing of joint measurement data, is tailored to cancel the effect of noise. Furthermore, the protocol is Hamiltonian-independent and robust to realistic ancilla noise. This work points to a promising direction for achieving high-fidelity analogue quantum simulation in the presence of noise.

item.title: DigiDent: integrated bristle-level sensing and AI for contact-aware toothbrushing assessment
item.description:
Nature Communications · Hao Ren, Hsin‐I Chang, Tak Nok Douglas Yu, Liu Yang, Tieshan Zhang, Gen Li
Oral hygiene is fundamental to systemic health, yet toothbrushing, the most common preventive practice, remains largely unguided and unquantified, contributing to the global burden of oral diseases. Current smart toothbrush systems fundamentally fail to capture the critical fine-scale biomechanics at the bristle-tooth interface, which is essential for evaluating clinical adherence and preventing gingival damage. Here we present DigiDent, an AI powered sensing to interpretation system that renders brushing micro-biomechanics computationally interpretable by measuring in-situ contact dynamics at bristle-tooth interface with an embedded E-Bristle sensor. DigiDent fuses bristle-level contact sensing with inertial sensing through a dual-stream neural inference architecture, converting contact-rich brushing behavior into quantitative and interpretable metrics of force, duration, contact-motion pattern, and fine-grained coverage. In validation experiments, DigiDent achieved >99% recognition of motion-contact patterns and 99.84% classification accuracy across 21 brushing subregions. Pilot user-operation verification further demonstrates the feasibility of DigiDent for real-use brushing monitoring and quantitative feedback. These results establish embedded co-deformation sensing and AI-based interpretation as a technical foundation for future personalized toothbrushing assessment and coaching. Oral hygiene is fundamental to systemic health, yet toothbrushing behavior remains largely unquantified because existing monitoring approaches cannot capture the distributed micro-contact dynamics within the bristle field. Here, the authors report DigiDent, a hardware-software co-designed framework combining embedded co-deformation sensing with AI-based analysis to quantify contact-rich brushing behavior. Pilot human studies demonstrate its potential for real-world brushing monitoring, personalized feedback, and habit assessment.

item.title: Short Wavelength Infrared Diimmonium Nano-Agents for Photoacoustic Imaging
item.description:
Nature Communications · Longcai Liu, Yang Chen, Liya Yu, Xiaozhou Mou, Guangxue Feng, Yu‐Dong Cai
Abstract Photoacoustic imaging (PAI) as an innovative biomedical imaging modality shows high contrast and superior spatial resolution, yet remains limited by underdeveloped second near-infrared (NIR-II, 1000-1700 nm) contrast agents, particularly neglecting the NIR-IIb (1500-1700 nm) window. In this work, we designed a new class of diimmonium (DB)-based dicationic nano-agents (DB·2X, X = TFSI - , B(C 2 O 4 ) 2 - , or BF 4 - ) for 1700 nm excitation PAI. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that dicationic DB 2+ exhibits a dramatically reduced excitation energy (1.24 eV) and enhanced oscillator strength (f = 1.11) by molecular engineering, attributed to a symmetry-allowed local excitation mechanism for electronic restructuring. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction further demonstrates the intermolecular spacings >5.0 Å in DB·2X aggregates, facilitating optimized non-radiative transitions for amplified PAI signals. In vivo study using different disease models shows that DB·2TFSI nano-agents under 1700 nm excitation can achieve higher signal-to-background ratio and minimized interference from endogenous chromophores compared to conventional 1064 nm excitation. Biocompatibility assessments confirm low cytotoxicity, underscoring potential for further development of DB·2TFSI nano-agents. This work delivers a robust molecular design paradigm for non-radiative decay optimization, and for the first time establishes 1700 nm-excitable PAI nano-agents, paving the way for tissue high-quality biomedical imaging.

item.title: Bias-reconfigurable barrier photodetectors for integrated broadband sensing and neuromorphic vision
item.description:
Nature Communications · Shizheng Wang, Fang Yang, Weiwei Zhao, Shijie Lang, Zhaofu Chen, Yinan Wang
Intelligent vision systems demand photodetectors with reconfigurable response to support diverse modalities like high-speed sensing and neuromorphic processing. Here we show a bias-reconfigurable barrier photodetector that enables continuous modulation of response time across 7 orders of magnitude, from 614 ns to 8.28 s. This wide-range tunability is achieved by electrically modulating the interfacial barrier height, which switches the dominant carrier transport mechanism from direct tunneling to barrier-limited thermal excitation and trap-assisted processes. Under low bias, the device functions as a high-speed photodetector, whereas elevated biases extend the response to synaptic timescales, enabling in-sensor neuromorphic computing as a physical reservoir. Notably, the device exhibits a broadband photoresponse from visible to mid-infrared. High accuracy was achieved in complex recognition tasks, such as classifying vehicle acceleration or deceleration. This integration of fast photodetection and neuromorphic computation establishes hardware-efficient paradigms for integrated machine vision, adaptive multispectral sensing, and energy-efficient edge intelligence. Intelligent vision systems require diverse functionalities, ranging from high-speed sensing to neuromorphic processing. Wang et al. report a reconfigurable photodetector that seamlessly switches between these two operating modes, with its response time continuously tunable from nanoseconds to seconds.
